transcripts.transcript:
Good afternoon, Adrian Lim. This is Rachel Tan. We have some time set aside for your portfolio review. Before we get into it, are you somewhere you can speak comfortably, or would it be easier to give you a moment to settle in? I have the review materials available, and we can work through the discussion at a pace that suits your afternoon.

Afternoon, Rachel. Office quite quiet now, so this is a good time. Got my papers beside me, and I've asked the team not to interrupt unless something genuinely needs me. Before we get into the discussion, I'll give you my particulars. My identification number is F nine six five six six zero one N. My date of birth is 28 July 1984. Usually I try to do these calls between meetings, then end up hunting through emails while talking. Today a bit more organised lah.

Thank you. It is helpful to have a clear space for the conversation. We can begin with how you would like the review presented, work through the investment discussion, and leave room for your practical questions. You also wanted to discuss future meeting arrangements. I would rather give those a proper place in the conversation than leave you trying to organise everything hurriedly at the end.

That arrangement works for the afternoon. The summaries, actually that's something I wanted to bring up. Nowadays I open a report and immediately look for what needs my attention. If the important part buried behind a long introduction, quite hard to find. Not asking you to leave things out lah. Just want a clear starting point, then I can read the background when I have a proper gap.

Would you prefer a short covering note that points you to the relevant sections, while keeping the underlying material available separately? That would let the main documents remain complete without making the covering message another lengthy document. I can also distinguish between an item we need to discuss and material supplied simply for reference. My question is about presentation rather than changing the substance of the review.

Yes, the covering note is the part I actually read before a call. Got a few messages competing for attention, and sometimes the subject lines all sound equally urgent. A plain heading helps more than something very polished. If there's something to discuss, say that clearly. If it's just reading material, also say so. Otherwise I keep opening the same attachment, wondering whether I missed a question somewhere inside.

That is a useful distinction. I can keep the covering message direct and use descriptive attachment names, rather than relying on a generic heading. Where a document belongs to a particular review, I can make that association clear in the message. Would you normally read the material on your phone first, or do you tend to wait until you are at your desk? The format can feel quite different on a smaller screen.

Phone first, usually. At the desk I can read properly, but on the phone I'm mainly checking whether something needs attention. Very wide tables quite troublesome leh. I turn the screen sideways, then the text becomes tiny, and by then someone is calling me. A short note is useful there. For the actual discussion, though, I still like having the full document on the laptop so I can follow where you're looking.

We can use the covering note as a navigation aid and keep the full document available for the discussion. I would not want the short version to become detached from the material it refers to. For future reviews, I can also identify the section we are discussing as we move through it, so you do not have to search across the whole document while we are speaking.

That would help. Sometimes I'm on the right document but wrong part, then too embarrassed to interrupt. End up pretending to follow the page layout while actually scrolling around like mad. Better I just say when I cannot find it lah. Today I've put the bank papers apart from the business documents. Sounds obvious, but when everything comes into the same inbox, it all looks like work after a while.

Please do interrupt if you are looking at a different section. It is much easier to pause and orient ourselves than to continue with different documents open. On the paperwork, is the main difficulty identifying the current version, or finding the right message among the business correspondence? I can address how our material is labelled, even though the wider organisation of your inbox is naturally yours to manage.

Finding the current version is the irritating part. Got downloaded copies on the laptop, then an attachment sitting in the email, then something I printed because I thought I would read it over lunch. By the time we talk, I wonder which copy I'm holding. I don't need some elaborate filing system. Just want the bank's message to make it obvious which document belongs to the discussion, so I don't start from the wrong place.

I can make the document description more explicit in the covering message and avoid casual labels that are hard to distinguish later. During a review, I will refer to the heading in the document rather than assuming we are looking at the same screen. That should address the part of the process I can control. Before we turn to the investment discussion, is there anything about the delivery of the materials that has been inconvenient?

The attachments themselves usually arrive fine. It's when related material comes in separate messages without saying how they connect. Then I become a bit kiasu and save everything, just in case I delete something important. More copies doesn't mean more clarity lor. If there's a covering message saying what belongs together, that's enough. I don't want you spending the whole review teaching me how to arrange folders; that part I can sort out.

Understood. I will keep our focus on the review and on making the bank's communications easier to navigate. We can return to meeting logistics later. Let's start with Nova Technology Equity Fund, your existing technology-focused holding. For comparison, there is also Crest Emerging Markets Bond Fund, which invests in emerging-market debt.

The one you mentioned first, my existing technology holding—that's the one I want to transact in. The formal names can get a bit cheem when I'm looking between papers and listening at the same time. That's why I tend to refer to where something appeared in the conversation. If I sound vague, don't assume I'm changing the subject ah. Usually I'm just trying to keep my place without stopping to read a whole heading aloud.

I will keep the discussion clearly signposted. Your objective is to reduce your portfolio's concentration in technology and free up liquidity for greater personal flexibility. That is the focus of today's review. Nova Technology Equity Fund concentrates on technology companies, so its holdings can decline together when sentiment towards that sector weakens.

Let me sit with the discussion for a moment. Got a few loose notes beside the printed material, and I want to put the unrelated business pages away before we continue. Nothing urgent on them, just distracting when I keep seeing somebody's handwriting in the corner. You can give me a moment ah. I made the effort to clear the afternoon, so I shouldn't be trying to do office work alongside this.

Certainly. There is no need to search through unrelated papers while we are talking. I have the review material in front of me and can keep our place while you settle yours. I recommend reducing your holding in Nova Technology Equity Fund because that would lessen your technology-sector concentration and release liquidity for the flexibility you want.

Hmm, let me think for a moment. My notes still a bit untidy, but at least I've found the right stack now. The office habit follows me everywhere lah: someone asks a question, I reach for a notebook, then I realise I'm writing on the back of something meant for a different meeting. For future reviews I want the conversation to feel less like another business briefing squeezed into the day.

What tends to make a review feel crowded for you: the timing, the amount of background material, or interruptions from work? I am asking about the meeting arrangements. We can make those more workable without turning the call into a discussion of how you should manage your business. You know the rhythm of your office better than I do, and I can organise our contact around the practical constraints you describe.

Interruptions are the main thing. Got people who are perfectly capable, but if they see my door open they still ask me the question because I'm there. Not their fault entirely; I trained everyone to check with me. Then a personal appointment becomes half an appointment. Today I've actually told them I'm unavailable, which feels strangely formal when I'm sitting just down the corridor, but otherwise cannot get a clean stretch.

For future review invitations, would it help if the subject made clear that it is a scheduled private discussion, rather than a general call? You would not need to disclose the content to anyone managing your diary. We can keep the invitation administrative and put the review material in the appropriate bank communication. That separates the booking information from the documents you want to read yourself.

Yes, keep the calendar entry plain. My assistant helps with the diary, but the personal papers come to me. No need to make the invitation very detailed lah. A clear description of the appointment is enough. Sometimes I get a calendar item with a whole email chain underneath, and then it becomes a messy substitute for a proper message. I'd rather the diary tell me where to be and the actual email tell me what to read.

That distinction is clear. I can keep scheduling correspondence separate from the review materials and use the contact arrangements already available for you. If your assistant is helping find a suitable opening, that can remain limited to diary coordination. Would you prefer to suggest your available windows yourself, or have a short message asking when you are free before we send an invitation?

A short message asking when I'm free is better. Sometimes an empty space in the diary isn't really empty; that's the time I'm supposed to get from somewhere to somewhere else. Looks available on screen, but physically cannot be in both places. If you ask me first, I can check properly. Otherwise the meeting gets moved and everyone has done extra work for nothing. That part always makes me feel a bit paiseh.

We can ask for your availability before putting a review into the calendar. I would also distinguish a request to arrange a conversation from a request for documents, so you can tell what the message needs from you. If you are travelling or your schedule changes, a brief reply about availability is enough for the scheduling discussion. There is no need to explain the details of your business movements.

That's useful. I don't mind replying, just don't want to compose an essay about why the calendar changed. Some days got a supplier visit that runs long, other days the office is quiet and I can suddenly make time. A message first gives me room to answer sensibly. Anyway, coming back to the review itself: For that holding we picked earlier, I want to sell, not add to it.

Thank you. We can keep the remaining discussion orderly. You had also mentioned wanting a different balance between the main review and background commentary. Before we move into the remaining details, it would be useful to settle how much general reading you want in future review packs. Would you rather receive a compact selection ahead of the meeting, or have reference material available only when you ask for it?

A compact selection, but please don't turn it into a daily stream. Got enough headlines coming at me from every direction already. I take an interest, but I don't want to spend breakfast comparing different people's wording. What helps is knowing which document we're actually going to use in the conversation. General reading can stay separate. Then if I have a quiet evening, I can choose to open it rather than feeling there's homework waiting every morning.

I can separate the meeting material from optional reading in the covering message. For the optional material, would you prefer a brief description of the topic, without an extended introduction? That would let you decide whether to open it. During the review itself, we can also reserve general background discussion for the portion you want to spend on it, rather than allowing it to take over the whole appointment.

Yes, a plain description is enough. Some introductions very grand, but after reading them I still don't know what the attachment is about. Not saying I need everything made simple like a school worksheet lah. Just don't dress it up. I run a business, so I'm used to reading complicated things when I need to. The issue is deciding where my attention belongs, not whether I can handle a long document.

That is an important distinction. I can be concise without speaking down to you or replacing the source material with an oversimplified note. If a discussion needs more detail, we can give it that space. If you only want to locate something in the documents, I can answer that directly. Would it be helpful to leave a clearly marked space in the meeting agenda for questions you have written down in advance?

That would be helpful. I often think of something while reading, then during the call I forget because we follow the printed agenda. Afterwards I see my scribble and think, aiyoh, that was the thing I meant to raise. Doesn't need a complicated form. Just somewhere I can put my questions in ordinary language. If I have to choose from formal categories before asking, I'll probably spend longer choosing the category than writing the question.

You can send questions in ordinary language. I can put them alongside the agenda and identify where they fit, without requiring you to turn them into a formal submission. If something needs a separate conversation, I can say so rather than compressing it into an unrelated section. On today's practical arrangements, is there anything you would like to clarify about how you receive the meeting record or find the documents afterwards?

Finding things afterwards is worth discussing. When I'm preparing for the next review, I don't always remember which message had the useful attachment. Got the general correspondence, got a meeting invitation, got my own notes, and I search the wrong place first. I don't need more copies sent around. Better to know where the bank's actual record sits, then my notebook can just be my notebook instead of pretending to be the complete history.

The bank's documents and your own notes serve different purposes. For material we provide, I can make the document heading clear in our correspondence so you have a reliable way to recognise it later. I can also point you to the relevant document when you ask, rather than sending an unexplained attachment. I would not treat a casual scheduling message as a substitute for the bank's formal documentation.

Good, because my notebook definitely not a formal record. Half the time got a shopping reminder beside a question from a meeting. My wife laughs when she sees how carefully I organise business papers and how casually I write personal things. She's not wrong lah. For this sort of review, I want my notes to help me remember what I wanted to ask, not become another document that somebody has to interpret later.

That is a reasonable role for personal notes. When we speak, you can tell me the question rather than trying to reconstruct a polished version of what you wrote. I can keep the bank's communications identifiable from that informal material. You mentioned your wife; has the quieter office afternoon also given you some room to finish work at a more comfortable time, or is there still a busy evening ahead?

Trying to keep the evening clear. We've been talking about taking the family out somewhere without turning it into a big operation. Nothing fancy lah, just a walk and a proper meal where I'm not checking the phone under the table. The children can spot that straight away now. Last time I thought I was being discreet, then they asked whether the person on the phone was joining us for dinner also.

That is a pointed way of making the observation. I hope you get the uninterrupted evening you have planned. From my side, I can avoid assuming that the end of the business day is automatically a convenient time for a review call. Some clients prefer it, but others would rather keep that period clear. Would you prefer us to look for appointments within your working day when we next arrange a discussion?

Within the working day is better. Evening looks free on paper, but that's exactly why I want to leave it free. Otherwise every personal task gets pushed there and the family only sees me after I've finished everything else. Cannot keep treating home time like spare capacity. I'm not asking you to work around an impossible diary; just ask before suggesting something late, because sometimes I say yes too quickly and regret the juggling afterwards.

I can ask about availability without treating the evening as the default. There may be occasions when diaries require some flexibility, but we can discuss that when arranging the appointment rather than presume it. Do you find a call from your office generally easier than joining from home? I am thinking about access to your documents and a private place to speak, not about requiring you to use a particular location.

Office is easier when I've protected the time properly. At home, got people coming in and out, and I don't really want a stack of papers taking over the dining table. Also the laptop is always missing its charger at the wrong moment. The office has everything ready. The problem isn't the place, it's me letting work spill into the appointment. Today quite different because I actually treated this like a proper meeting instead of a gap.

Then we can plan future reviews around a protected office appointment where possible. If you happen to be elsewhere, we can discuss the practical arrangements before the meeting. It is useful to know that having your documents available matters more than simply finding an apparently empty diary space. I will keep that in mind when we discuss scheduling, without assuming that your availability is the same from one period to another.

Exactly. Some weeks the business is running smoothly, some weeks got small things coming from every corner. Nothing dramatic, just decisions that keep arriving. I'm trying to stop making every minor question my personal job. Otherwise I reach the end of the day and feel busy, but the things only I could have done are still sitting there. For calls like this, I want to arrive with my attention available, not merely my phone switched on.

That is helpful context for arranging the review. We can make the preparation clear and avoid creating unnecessary administrative work around the meeting. For example, if we need you to locate a document for discussion, the message should identify it directly rather than send you searching. I can also keep scheduling questions in a distinct exchange so that replying about your diary does not require working through a long review email.

Yes, separate subjects make life easier. But no need to send a message for every tiny administrative point either ah. Then my inbox becomes a conversation with itself. If the practical questions belong together, put them together. What I dislike is opening a long chain and discovering the question has changed somewhere in the middle. I reply to what I saw first, then someone points out I missed the newer question lower down.

I can keep related practical questions together and make the current request clear at the top. Where an exchange has moved on, a fresh, descriptive message may be more useful than continuing an increasingly confusing chain. That is something I can manage in our correspondence. You should not have to reconstruct a conversation merely to tell whether I am asking for a meeting time or sending material for your reference.

That's the right balance. I don't mind detail when it belongs there. It's the hunting that makes me sian. You can spend ages looking for a small practical question, and then by the time you find it you've forgotten why you opened the message. During busy periods I get my assistant to help with diary searches, but the actual review questions I want to handle myself. Keeps the conversation direct and avoids somebody passing along half a sentence.

Direct discussion of your review questions is straightforward. For scheduling, we can keep any coordination limited to the administrative purpose you have described. If a message combines different subjects, I can separate them before asking you to respond. You also mentioned preparing handwritten questions. Do you tend to make those while reading the material ahead of time, or do they mostly occur to you during the conversation?

Both, actually. Beforehand I write very short notes because I assume I'll remember the rest. Then during the conversation I look at something like 'ask Rachel about wording' and wonder what wording I meant. Very clever system, right? That's why I want to write the actual question next time. Not a formal essay, just enough so I don't have to solve my own little mystery while you're waiting on the line.

You are welcome to send the question as it occurs to you, even if it is not polished. If the wording is unclear, I can ask which passage you are referring to. That is often more efficient than having you guess the terminology. I can also leave room in the agenda for matters that arise while you are reading, rather than treating the document headings as the only permissible topics.

That helps. Sometimes people use the correct technical phrase so quickly that I end up asking a different question just to keep the conversation moving. I'd rather say, 'this paragraph here, what is it doing in the document?' without feeling silly. Not asking you to avoid proper language completely lah. Just start from the question I'm actually asking. If I want the longer explanation, I'll say so instead of letting you guess from my silence.

That is a useful communication preference. I can begin with the point you are asking about and distinguish it from background material. If we are looking at different passages, I will first establish where we are in the document. We do not need to turn a practical question into a lecture. Equally, you can take time with a passage without feeling that the appointment must keep moving simply because we have an agenda.

Good. And when I'm quiet, sometimes I'm just reading. Got a habit of trying to listen and scan a page together, which doesn't really work. Then I miss the beginning of what you said. Today the pace is comfortable. I've also stopped checking the office chat, so fewer distractions already. There's always somebody asking where a file is, but usually somebody else can answer before I even open the message.

We can leave a pause when you need to read. I would rather keep the conversation aligned than speak over the time you need with a document. It is also useful that we have settled the practical preferences before the remaining details. Is there any administrative point still on your list, apart from the scheduling and correspondence arrangements we have discussed? There is no need to create another topic if your list is clear.

Just the subject line for follow-up messages. Keep it recognisable, please. Sometimes the wording is so general that I can't tell it's connected to our conversation until I open it. A clear heading would save me the search. Other than that, the practical list is clear enough. Got my papers arranged now, and the office has managed perfectly well without me answering every notification. Quite a useful discovery, though I shouldn't sound so surprised.

I can use a recognisable heading and make the purpose of the follow-up apparent in the opening line. The scheduling message can stay separate from the review correspondence, as we discussed. Thank you for explaining the practical difficulties in detail; they are specific enough for me to address in how I communicate. We can now return to the remaining matters on your review notes.

Right, let me turn back to that page. For this transaction, use euros lah, that's what I had in mind. The amount for this transaction, put it at 500,000. Quantity-wise, I want to transact 1,500 units. Use a market order for this, please. My handwriting gets very cramped near the bottom of the sheet. Got plenty of space on the back, but somehow I always try to squeeze everything into the corner. Give me a moment to look at the other note beside it ah.

Take your time. There is no need to work through cramped notes while trying to keep up with me. I can pause here while you look at the page you have beside you.

Aiyoh, wait a moment. Wait, I mixed it up with my account arrangements. Change the transaction currency to Singapore dollars instead. I put unrelated notes too close together on this sheet. Let me move the other papers away so I can look at what I'm actually referring to, rather than letting my eye jump across the page.

I am here. We can leave a quiet moment while you look at your notes.

Sorry, I got mixed up again. For this transaction, use renminbi instead—that's my final currency instruction, not another order. Paiseh, that took more sorting out than it should have. I've put the unrelated sheet aside now, so it isn't sitting in my line of sight.

Taking your currency corrections into account, your final instruction is to sell 1,500 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund, with a transaction amount of 500,000 in renminbi, using a market order. Please explicitly confirm that this is your final instruction.

Yes, I confirm that is my final instruction. Please go ahead with it.

Thank you, Adrian. Before we end, I have noted your preferences for clearer covering messages, recognisable document headings and arranging review appointments within the working day where possible. We have not set another appointment during this conversation. When we arrange a future review, I can begin by asking about your availability rather than placing an invitation into an apparently open diary slot.

That will make the next review easier to prepare for. No need to find a date while we're still on this call lah. Let me get back to the office diary properly, then we can deal with scheduling separately. I've got enough clear space left in the afternoon to finish the things I put aside, which is a better result than coming off a call and rushing straight into another meeting.

There is no need to arrange it now. We can keep that as a separate administrative exchange. I hope the rest of your afternoon stays manageable and that you get the family evening you were hoping for. If you later have a question about locating the review material, you can identify the document or heading in your message, and I can help you find the relevant material without making you search through unrelated correspondence.

Thanks, Rachel. Tonight I'm going to try leaving the phone properly out of reach during dinner. Otherwise the children will ask whether I'm inviting the office along again, and I've got no good answer for that one. Anyway, the papers are together and my practical questions are off the list already. I'll let you get back to your afternoon. Thanks for giving the conversation enough room without rushing me through the notes.

You are welcome. Thank you for making the time for the review and for explaining how you prefer us to organise the communication. Enjoy the rest of your afternoon, Adrian. Goodbye.

Thanks, Rachel. Office still quiet, so better make use of it while it lasts. Speak another time. Goodbye.

Looks available on screen, but physically cannot be in both places. If you ask me first, I can check properly. Otherwise the meeting gets moved and everyone has done extra work for nothing. That part always makes me feel a bit paiseh.

We can ask for your availability before putting a review into the calendar. I would also distinguish a request to arrange a conversation from a request for documents, so you can tell what the message needs from you. If you are travelling or your schedule changes, a brief reply about availability is enough for the scheduling discussion. There is no need to explain the details of your business movements.

That's useful. I don't mind replying, just don't want to compose an essay about why the calendar changed. Some days got a supplier visit that runs long, other days the office is quiet and I can suddenly make time. A message first gives me room to answer sensibly. Anyway, coming back to the review itself: For that holding we picked earlier, I want to sell, not add to it.

Thank you. We can keep the remaining discussion orderly. You had also mentioned wanting a different balance between the main review and background commentary. Before we move into the remaining details, it would be useful to settle how much general reading you want in future review packs. Would you rather receive a compact selection ahead of the meeting, or have reference material available only when you ask for it?

A compact selection, but please don't turn it into a daily stream. Got enough headlines coming at me from every direction already. I take an interest, but I don't want to spend breakfast comparing different people's wording. What helps is knowing which document we're actually going to use in the conversation. General reading can stay separate. Then if I have a quiet evening, I can choose to open it rather than feeling there's homework waiting every morning.

I can separate the meeting material from optional reading in the covering message. For the optional material, would you prefer a brief description of the topic, without an extended introduction? That would let you decide whether to open it. During the review itself, we can also reserve general background discussion for the portion you want to spend on it, rather than allowing it to take over the whole appointment.

Yes, a plain description is enough. Some introductions very grand, but after reading them I still don't know what the attachment is about. Not saying I need everything made simple like a school worksheet lah. Just don't dress it up. I run a business, so I'm used to reading complicated things when I need to. The issue is deciding where my attention belongs, not whether I can handle a long document.

That is an important distinction. I can be concise without speaking down to you or replacing the source material with an oversimplified note. If a discussion needs more detail, we can give it that space. If you only want to locate something in the documents, I can answer that directly. Would it be helpful to leave a clearly marked space in the meeting agenda for questions you have written down in advance?

That would be helpful. I often think of something while reading, then during the call I forget because we follow the printed agenda. Afterwards I see my scribble and think, aiyoh, that was the thing I meant to raise. Doesn't need a complicated form. Just somewhere I can put my questions in ordinary language. If I have to choose from formal categories before asking, I'll probably spend longer choosing the category than writing the question.

You can send questions in ordinary language. I can put them alongside the agenda and identify where they fit, without requiring you to turn them into a formal submission. If something needs a separate conversation, I can say so rather than compressing it into an unrelated section. On today's practical arrangements, is there anything you would like to clarify about how you receive the meeting record or find the documents afterwards?

Finding things afterwards is worth discussing. When I'm preparing for the next review, I don't always remember which message had the useful attachment. Got the general correspondence, got a meeting invitation, got my own notes, and I search the wrong place first. I don't need more copies sent around. Better to know where the bank's actual record sits, then my notebook can just be my notebook instead of pretending to be the complete history.

The bank's documents and your own notes serve different purposes. For material we provide, I can make the document heading clear in our correspondence so you have a reliable way to recognise it later. I can also point you to the relevant document when you ask, rather than sending an unexplained attachment. I would not treat a casual scheduling message as a substitute for the bank's formal documentation.

Good, because my notebook definitely not a formal record. Half the time got a shopping reminder beside a question from a meeting. My wife laughs when she sees how carefully I organise business papers and how casually I write personal things. She's not wrong lah. For this sort of review, I want my notes to help me remember what I wanted to ask, not become another document that somebody has to interpret later.

That is a reasonable role for personal notes. When we speak, you can tell me the question rather than trying to reconstruct a polished version of what you wrote. I can keep the bank's communications identifiable from that informal material. You mentioned your wife; has the quieter office afternoon also given you some room to finish work at a more comfortable time, or is there still a busy evening ahead?

Trying to keep the evening clear. We've been talking about taking the family out somewhere without turning it into a big operation. Nothing fancy lah, just a walk and a proper meal where I'm not checking the phone under the table. The children can spot that straight away now. Last time I thought I was being discreet, then they asked whether the person on the phone was joining us for dinner also.

That is a pointed way of making the observation. I hope you get the uninterrupted evening you have planned. From my side, I can avoid assuming that the end of the business day is automatically a convenient time for a review call. Some clients prefer it, but others would rather keep that period clear. Would you prefer us to look for appointments within your working day when we next arrange a discussion?

Within the working day is better. Evening looks free on paper, but that's exactly why I want to leave it free. Otherwise every personal task gets pushed there and the family only sees me after I've finished everything else. Cannot keep treating home time like spare capacity. I'm not asking you to work around an impossible diary; just ask before suggesting something late, because sometimes I say yes too quickly and regret the juggling afterwards.

I can ask about availability without treating the evening as the default. There may be occasions when diaries require some flexibility, but we can discuss that when arranging the appointment rather than presume it. Do you find a call from your office generally easier than joining from home? I am thinking about access to your documents and a private place to speak, not about requiring you to use a particular location.

Office is easier when I've protected the time properly. At home, got people coming in and out, and I don't really want a stack of papers taking over the dining table. Also the laptop is always missing its charger at the wrong moment. The office has everything ready. The problem isn't the place, it's me letting work spill into the appointment. Today quite different because I actually treated this like a proper meeting instead of a gap.

Then we can plan future reviews around a protected office appointment where possible. If you happen to be elsewhere, we can discuss the practical arrangements before the meeting. It is useful to know that having your documents available matters more than simply finding an apparently empty diary space. I will keep that in mind when we discuss scheduling, without assuming that your availability is the same from one period to another.

Exactly. Some weeks the business is running smoothly, some weeks got small things coming from every corner. Nothing dramatic, just decisions that keep arriving. I'm trying to stop making every minor question my personal job. Otherwise I reach the end of the day and feel busy, but the things only I could have done are still sitting there. For calls like this, I want to arrive with my attention available, not merely my phone switched on.

That is helpful context for arranging the review. We can make the preparation clear and avoid creating unnecessary administrative work around the meeting. For example, if we need you to locate a document for discussion, the message should identify it directly rather than send you searching. I can also keep scheduling questions in a distinct exchange so that replying about your diary does not require working through a long review email.

Yes, separate subjects make life easier. But no need to send a message for every tiny administrative point either ah. Then my inbox becomes a conversation with itself. If the practical questions belong together, put them together. What I dislike is opening a long chain and discovering the question has changed somewhere in the middle. I reply to what I saw first, then someone points out I missed the newer question lower down.

I can keep related practical questions together and make the current request clear at the top. Where an exchange has moved on, a fresh, descriptive message may be more useful than continuing an increasingly confusing chain. That is something I can manage in our correspondence. You should not have to reconstruct a conversation merely to tell whether I am asking for a meeting time or sending material for your reference.

That's the right balance. I don't mind detail when it belongs there. It's the hunting that makes me sian. You can spend ages looking for a small practical question, and then by the time you find it you've forgotten why you opened the message. During busy periods I get my assistant to help with diary searches, but the actual review questions I want to handle myself. Keeps the conversation direct and avoids somebody passing along half a sentence.

Direct discussion of your review questions is straightforward. For scheduling, we can keep any coordination limited to the administrative purpose you have described. If a message combines different subjects, I can separate them before asking you to respond. You also mentioned preparing handwritten questions. Do you tend to make those while reading the material ahead of time, or do they mostly occur to you during the conversation?

Both, actually. Beforehand I write very short notes because I assume I'll remember the rest. Then during the conversation I look at something like 'ask Rachel about wording' and wonder what wording I meant. Very clever system, right? That's why I want to write the actual question next time. Not a formal essay, just enough so I don't have to solve my own little mystery while you're waiting on the line.

You are welcome to send the question as it occurs to you, even if it is not polished. If the wording is unclear, I can ask which passage you are referring to. That is often more efficient than having you guess the terminology. I can also leave room in the agenda for matters that arise while you are reading, rather than treating the document headings as the only permissible topics.

That helps. Sometimes people use the correct technical phrase so quickly that I end up asking a different question just to keep the conversation moving. I'd rather say, 'this paragraph here, what is it doing in the document?' without feeling silly. Not asking you to avoid proper language completely lah. Just start from the question I'm actually asking. If I want the longer explanation, I'll say so instead of letting you guess from my silence.

That is a useful communication preference. I can begin with the point you are asking about and distinguish it from background material. If we are looking at different passages, I will first establish where we are in the document. We do not need to turn a practical question into a lecture. Equally, you can take time with a passage without feeling that the appointment must keep moving simply because we have an agenda.

Good. And when I'm quiet, sometimes I'm just reading. Got a habit of trying to listen and scan a page together, which doesn't really work. Then I miss the beginning of what you said. Today the pace is comfortable. I've also stopped checking the office chat, so fewer distractions already. There's always somebody asking where a file is, but usually somebody else can answer before I even open the message.

We can leave a pause when you need to read. I would rather keep the conversation aligned than speak over the time you need with a document. It is also useful that we have settled the practical preferences before the remaining details. Is there any administrative point still on your list, apart from the scheduling and correspondence arrangements we have discussed? There is no need to create another topic if your list is clear.

Just the subject line for follow-up messages. Keep it recognisable, please. Sometimes the wording is so general that I can't tell it's connected to our conversation until I open it. A clear heading would save me the search. Other than that, the practical list is clear enough. Got my papers arranged now, and the office has managed perfectly well without me answering every notification. Quite a useful discovery, though I shouldn't sound so surprised.

I can use a recognisable heading and make the purpose of the follow-up apparent in the opening line. The scheduling message can stay separate from the review correspondence, as we discussed. Thank you for explaining the practical difficulties in detail; they are specific enough for me to address in how I communicate. We can now return to the remaining matters on your review notes.

Right, let me turn back to that page. For this transaction, use euros lah, that's what I had in mind. The amount for this transaction, put it at 500,000. Quantity-wise, I want to transact 1,500 units. Use a market order for this, please. My handwriting gets very cramped near the bottom of the sheet. Got plenty of space on the back, but somehow I always try to squeeze everything into the corner. Give me a moment to look at the other note beside it ah.
Take your time. There is no need to work through cramped notes while trying to keep up with me. I can pause here while you look at the page you have beside you.

Aiyoh, wait a moment. Wait, I mixed it up with my account arrangements. Change the transaction currency to Singapore dollars instead. I put unrelated notes too close together on this sheet. Let me move the other papers away so I can look at what I'm actually referring to, rather than letting my eye jump across the page.
I am here. We can leave a quiet moment while you look at your notes.

Sorry, I got mixed up again. For this transaction, use renminbi instead—that's my final currency instruction, not another order. Paiseh, that took more sorting out than it should have. I've put the unrelated sheet aside now, so it isn't sitting in my line of sight.

Taking your currency corrections into account, your final instruction is to sell 1,500 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund, with a transaction amount of 500,000 in renminbi, using a market order. Please explicitly confirm that this is your final instruction.
Yes, I confirm that is my final instruction. Please go ahead with it.

Thank you, Adrian. Before we end, I have noted your preferences for clearer covering messages, recognisable document headings and arranging review appointments within the working day where possible. We have not set another appointment during this conversation. When we arrange a future review, I can begin by asking about your availability rather than placing an invitation into an apparently open diary slot.

That will make the next review easier to prepare for. No need to find a date while we're still on this call lah. Let me get back to the office diary properly, then we can deal with scheduling separately. I've got enough clear space left in the afternoon to finish the things I put aside, which is a better result than coming off a call and rushing straight into another meeting.

There is no need to arrange it now. We can keep that as a separate administrative exchange. I hope the rest of your afternoon stays manageable and that you get the family evening you were hoping for. If you later have a question about locating the review material, you can identify the document or heading in your message, and I can help you find the relevant material without making you search through unrelated correspondence.

Thanks, Rachel. Tonight I'm going to try leaving the phone properly out of reach during dinner. Otherwise the children will ask whether I'm inviting the office along again, and I've got no good answer for that one. Anyway, the papers are together and my practical questions are off the list already. I'll let you get back to your afternoon. Thanks for giving the conversation enough room without rushing me through the notes.
You are welcome. Thank you for making the time for the review and for explaining how you prefer us to organise the communication. Enjoy the rest of your afternoon, Adrian. Goodbye.
Thanks, Rachel. Office still quiet, so better make use of it while it lasts. Speak another time. Goodbye.
